# The March 28, 2020 Jonesboro Tornado

On Saturday, March 28, 2020, a powerful tornado struck Jonesboro, Arkansas, causing extensive destruction across the city , . Officially rated an EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale, the storm formed in southeast Jonesboro and tracked northeast through populated areas before dissipating just sixteen minutes later , . Despite the tornado's intensity and its path directly through homes and businesses, it resulted in zero fatalities, a remarkable outcome attributed in part to the concurrent COVID-19 pandemic which reduced occupancy in public spaces , , . The event caused catastrophic damage to key commercial properties, most notably The Mall at Turtle Creek, and inflicted an estimated $300 million to $500 million in economic losses , . The aftermath prompted significant emergency response efforts, a protracted recovery spanning years, and a fundamental transformation of the city's commercial landscape following the eventual demolition and sale of the damaged mall property , . The event serves as a case study in meteorological phenomena, disaster response, and the complex interplay between natural hazards and societal context.

## Meteorological Conditions and Event Characteristics

The tornado that impacted Jonesboro on March 28, 2020, developed within a highly unstable atmospheric environment conducive to severe thunderstorms and tornadogenesis . It occurred during Arkansas's peak tornado season and within the typical daily window for such events, just before 5:00 p.m. Central Daylight Time (CDT) . The National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center had issued a "Particularly Dangerous Situation" tornado watch for parts of the region earlier that day, highlighting the elevated risk . The meteorological setup featured several critical ingredients for a damaging tornado. A rapidly intensifying low-pressure system brought unseasonably warm and moist air into the area, while a strong low-level jet increased wind speeds to between 30 and 45 knots at approximately 5,000 feet above mean sea level over northeast Arkansas during the afternoon hours , . At 2100 UTC (4:00 p.m. CDT), localized parameters near Jonesboro indicated a mixed-layer convective available potential energy (MLCAPE) greater than 75 J/kg and storm-relative helicity (SRH) in the 0–1 km layer ranging from 150 to 190 m²/s², both favorable for rotating updrafts necessary for tornado formation . A crucial factor was the presence of a subtle eastward-drifting boundary, analyzed by the NWS as a cold front, which stalled near Jonesboro and provided critical low-level convergence and shear that likely contributed to the tornado's development .

The tornado itself touched down around 4:57 or 4:58 p.m. CDT on March 28, 2020 , . The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning at 4:47 p.m. CDT, providing residents with a ten-minute lead time before the tornado was visually confirmed moving across the city . The storm was short-lived but intensely destructive, lasting only 16 minutes before dissipating at approximately 5:14 p.m. CDT . Its path was relatively narrow but concentrated its power along a 20.20 km (12.55 miles) track , . The maximum width of the tornado was recorded at 550 meters (approximately 600 yards or one-third of a mile) , . The storm originated in southeast Jonesboro and moved in a northeast direction, impacting a densely populated corridor of the city . The event was documented by multiple sources, including the NOAA Storm Events Database, which serves as the authoritative record for official storm data compiled by the National Weather Service . The National Weather Service office in Memphis, Tennessee, was responsible for the official rating and assessment of the storm .

The primary measure of the tornado's intensity is the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale, which was adopted by the National Weather Service in 2007 . An independent structural engineering firm, Haag Engineering Company, also conducted a detailed damage survey in November 2022, using advanced methods like Google Street View and historical imagery to assess damage that had been obscured by rapid post-event cleanup . Their survey, titled 'Damage survey of the Jonesboro, Arkansas tornado: March 28, 2020', provided specific wind speed estimates for individual structures, revealing that damage varied significantly depending on construction type and location . For instance, they estimated winds of 110 mph (equivalent to an EF1 rating) at Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen, while other structures sustained far more severe damage . This highlights how the overall rating represents a composite of the most intense impacts along the path. The official rating of EF3 indicates estimated peak winds of 136 to 140 mph (61 to 62 m/s) , . This rating was determined during a rapid damage survey conducted by NWS personnel on March 29, 2020, the day after the event . The survey utilized the Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT) and involved over 80 scientists working to standardize the application of the EF scale . The immediate post-event cleanup complicated documentation, making damage details "perishable" and underscoring the challenges faced by surveyors . The event also exposed gaps in the EF scale's coverage for large shopping malls, prompting future updates to damage indicators .

## Damage Assessment and Structural Impact

The EF3 tornado unleashed catastrophic damage as it traversed Jonesboro, leaving a trail of destruction across hundreds of buildings . The most severely affected structure was The Mall at Turtle Creek, which suffered catastrophic damage that rendered a significant portion of the building uninhabitable and ultimately led to its demolition , . Employees who sheltered in an interior break room inside the mall confirmed that the room remained intact while the surrounding structure collapsed, illustrating the extreme forces at play . The damage included the complete loss of the roof in the mall's center section, collapsed exterior walls, widespread ceiling collapse, shattered storefront windows, and the destruction of numerous shops stretching from Dillard’s to Target . City code enforcement officers later declared the damaged eastern portion of the mall, extending from Victoria’s Secret to Dillard’s, a public hazard against public health and safety, effectively marking it for demolition , . The mall, which opened in 2006, was the largest enclosed mall in northeast Arkansas and had been the only new enclosed mall constructed in the United States that year .

In addition to the mall, the tornado inflicted severe damage at Jonesboro Municipal Airport, where hangars and airplanes were destroyed , , . Associated gusts from the tornado were powerful enough to derail a train . Other retail establishments also suffered extensive damage, with some buildings, including Ulta and Kirkland stores, collapsing completely . The storm's path through residential neighborhoods resulted in the destruction or severe damage of over 140 homes and more than 100 businesses overall , . One source noted EF-2 damage at the Turtle Creek Mall prior to it strengthening to EF-3 as the tornado continued northeast . The damage was so severe that the Dean B. Ellis Library closed early to allow staff to comply with a city-wide curfew implemented after the storm . The campus of nearby Arkansas State University experienced only minor damage, but at least three employees lost their homes, and many students residing in the area suffered similar housing damage .

The independent damage survey conducted by Haag Engineering in November 2022 provided a granular analysis of the structural failures observed . By utilizing Google Street View and historical imagery to circumvent the challenges of post-storm cleanup, the survey team was able to document specific wind speed estimates and patterns of failure across various types of structures . Their work highlighted the complexities of assessing tornado damage, particularly for large, modern commercial buildings like shopping malls, which have different construction characteristics compared to single-family homes . The survey found that most of the most severe damage occurred at the airport and the aforementioned retail stores, confirming the NWS's high-end EF3 rating for those locations . The report meticulously documented structural failures across residential, industrial, and commercial sites, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of the tornado's impact than a single, generalized EF rating could provide . This detailed engineering perspective revealed that while the official rating was based on the worst-case scenario observed, the actual wind field was likely variable, with different structures experiencing different levels of force along the tornado's path . This variability underscores the difficulty in assigning a precise and uniform wind speed to the entire storm, reinforcing the value of comprehensive, multi-point damage surveys for accurately characterizing such events.

## Human Toll and Emergency Response

Despite the tornado's EF3 intensity and its direct path through populated parts of Jonesboro, the most striking outcome was the absence of fatalities , , . The number of injuries is reported inconsistently across various sources, with figures cited as 18, 22, and at least 22 people injured , , . The higher figure of 22 injuries is supported by multiple reports and will be considered the most accurate count , . Multiple sources attribute this remarkably positive casualty outcome directly to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and the social distancing measures in place at the time , , . With many residents staying home due to lockdown orders and public businesses operating under reduced capacity, the population density in vulnerable indoor spaces like malls and offices was significantly lower than it would have been on a normal day , . This reduction in occupancy likely prevented a much higher death toll, turning a potentially deadly event into one with zero lives lost , . The effectiveness of the tornado warning dissemination via NOAA Weather Radio, cell alerts, and local media also played a critical role in allowing residents to seek shelter in time .

The human stories from the event illustrate both the tragedy and resilience of the community. Lucas Luster, a driver for the Jonesboro Fire Department, called his family moments before the tornado hit his house, which was subsequently destroyed . Fortunately, all his family members survived . Another compelling account comes from Sharon Gore, who was at her home near the mall with her adult son, Preston, who has nonverbal autism. During the tornado warning, she used Oreo mini cookies, a known behavioral intervention for him, to coax him from his fixed "dinner chair" so they could move to a safer back bedroom . Her experience provides a vivid example of adaptive behavior under extreme stress and the importance of personalized safety plans for individuals with special needs . After the storm passed, her son's missing dinner chair was found intact but blown out onto the yard, offering a poignant illustration of the localized and chaotic nature of wind forces during a tornado .

The emergency response in Jonesboro was swift and continuous. First responders were activated immediately upon the tornado warning . Jonesboro Fire Chief Marty Hamrick described responding to the event while watching movies with his own family, expecting a high number of casualties given the tornado's path through heavily populated areas . All four personnel units of the fire department were deployed during the incident, and firefighters worked continuously throughout the night and into the next day to recover people and manage the aftermath . Search and rescue operations were underway at The Mall at Turtle Creek, according to E-911 Director Jeff Presley . By the morning of March 29, 2020, the day after the tornado, the fire department reported that "everybody was accounted for," a testament to the effective warning systems and public response . In the immediate aftermath, the city implemented a city-wide curfew from 9 p.m. to daylight to maintain order and ensure public safety amidst widespread power outages and debris , . The Craighead County Office of Emergency Management did not pre-activate its emergency plans because the criteria for activation were not met prior to the storm; however, it did activate its emergency operations center five times for subsequent storm warnings in the period following the tornado, indicating a reactive learning process . Following the event, the Jonesboro Fire Department specifically refined its severe weather response plan, emphasizing the need for pre-identified staging areas for incoming mutual aid to improve coordination during future disasters .

## Economic Consequences and Federal Assistance

The economic impact of the March 28, 2020 tornado was profound, inflicting hundreds of millions of dollars in damage on the city of Jonesboro and Craighead County , . Estimates of the total damage varied between official state figures and private assessments. State officials, in their request for federal assistance, estimated the total damages from the tornado and associated severe storms at nearly $500 million , . Governor Asa Hutchinson stated the figure was "almost half a billion dollars in damage to the City of Jonesboro," a sum deemed sufficient to qualify for a major federal disaster declaration . A separate, independent estimate placed the economic losses at $300 million (in 2020 USD) . These figures encompass the extensive damage to residential properties, commercial buildings like The Mall at Turtle Creek, the municipal airport, and other infrastructure , . The financial burden of such a disaster created significant compounding stress for the community, as the economic impact from the tornado coincided with the economic downturn caused by the COVID-19 pandemic .

The severity of the damage and the scale of the recovery effort justified a major federal disaster declaration. President Donald Trump approved a declaration for Jonesboro and Craighead County in late April 2020, enabling FEMA public assistance programs to aid individuals, households, government agencies, and utilities . The formal request for federal aid was submitted by Arkansas in early April 2020, citing both the direct impacts of the tornadoes and the broader economic stress resulting from the concurrent pandemic . This federal assistance was crucial for funding the extensive cleanup and rebuilding processes. Key city infrastructure and services, including Jonesboro Municipal Airport, City Water & Light, and Craighead Electric, became eligible for federal support . The approval of the declaration underscored the systemic nature of the damage, which extended beyond individual homes and businesses to critical public services essential for the community's functioning and recovery . The preliminary damage assessment (PDA) process, coordinated by FEMA with state and local partners, was initiated to formally document the extent of the damage and validate the need for this federal aid . This process involves phases of local and state verification of damage to determine the magnitude of the disaster and inform decisions about major disaster declarations .

The long-term economic repercussions were significant, particularly for the local commercial sector. The prolonged closure and eventual demolition of The Mall at Turtle Creek represented a substantial blow to the regional economy, affecting employment and consumer activity , . The city's efforts to manage the aftermath of the mall's destruction were a central focus of its economic recovery strategy. Mayor Harold Copenhaver, who took office in January 2021, prioritized restoring full mall operations, especially from the west side outward, citing concerns about the unrepaired site being an "eyesore" and a danger to the community . The city's proactive management of the blighted property, from issuing notices to the owner to planning for demolition, demonstrated a strategic approach to mitigating the long-term negative effects on public safety and economic development , . The eventual sale of the land in September 2023 for redevelopment signaled a new chapter for the property, with plans for a 96,000-square-foot open-air power center projected to begin construction in 2026 . This multi-year transition from devastation to redevelopment highlights the enduring economic legacy of the tornado on the city's commercial landscape.

## Aftermath, Recovery, and Long-Term Repercussions

The aftermath of the March 28, 2020 tornado was characterized by a slow and methodical recovery process that spanned several years, fundamentally altering the physical and economic landscape of Jonesboro , . The immediate priority was clearing debris and ensuring public safety, which led to the implementation of a city-wide curfew , . However, the most visible and impactful aspect of the recovery was the fate of The Mall at Turtle Creek. Recognizing the structural compromise of the damaged sections, city officials took decisive action. In January 2021, approximately ten months after the tornado, Mayor Harold Copenhaver issued a 30-day notice to Brookfield Properties, the Chicago-based owner of the mall, requiring them to submit a remediation plan , . Failure to comply would trigger city council action, potentially leading to mandatory demolition under a 60-day demolition permit requirement . This enforcement action was driven by the city's desire to address the unrepaired site, which was designated a public hazard and nuisance against public health , .

Demolition of the most severely damaged central section of the mall began on March 15, 2021 , . The city's engineering assessment concluded that while the internal structure was sound, the extensive roof damage, water intrusion, and missing drywall made the section unsalvageable . The removal of the blighted section was a critical step in revitalizing the property. The remaining anchor stores—Dillard’s, JCPenney, and Target—remained operational on perimeter outparcels, serving as a base for future redevelopment , . The property itself eventually changed hands. On September 10, 2023, the land was sold at an online auction for $4.85 million to Turtle Creek Jonesboro LLC, an entity potentially led by real estate investor Keith Bayird of Paragould . This sale marked the beginning of a new era for the site, with a redevelopment plan announced for a 96,000-square-foot open-air power center . Construction on this new development is estimated to begin in 2026, representing a projected timeline of over six years from the initial disaster to the start of reconstruction .

This protracted recovery process illustrates the long shadow cast by a major disaster. The event not only caused immediate destruction but also necessitated years of planning, legal action, and investment to restore the area to a functional and safe condition. The story of The Mall at Turtle Creek's transformation from a catastrophic damage site to a redeveloped commercial hub is emblematic of the city's resilience. The redevelopment plan aims to create a modern retail space that replaces the outdated enclosed mall, reflecting a shift in commercial real estate trends even before the tornado struck . Furthermore, the tornado prompted tangible improvements in local emergency management protocols. The Jonesboro Fire Department, having witnessed the chaos firsthand, refined its severe weather response plan, placing a stronger emphasis on the identification of pre-designated staging areas for incoming mutual aid to streamline future disaster response efforts . In summary, the March 28, 2020 tornado was not merely a single event but a catalyst for a multi-faceted recovery that reshaped the city's infrastructure, economy, and preparedness strategies for years to come.

Turtle Creek Jonesboro LLC is an entity potentially led by real estate investor Keith Bayird of Paragould.
A redevelopment plan was announced for a 96,000-square-foot open-air power center.
Construction on this new development is estimated to begin in 2026.
The estimated construction start in 2026 represents a projected timeline of over six years from the initial disaster to the start of reconstruction.
The redevelopment plan aims to create a modern retail space that replaces the outdated enclosed mall.
The redevelopment plan reflects a shift in commercial real estate trends even before the tornado struck.
The tornado prompted tangible improvements in local emergency management protocols.

The Jonesboro Fire Department refined its severe weather response plan, placing a stronger emphasis on the identification of pre-designated staging areas for incoming mutual aid to streamline future disaster response efforts.

Click here for more information.") From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
2020 Jonesboro tornado

A traffic camera still of the tornado shortly after forming in Jonesboro

Meteorological history
FormedMarch 28, 2020, 4:58 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)
DissipatedMarch 28, 2020, 5:14 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)
Duration16 minutes
EF3 tornado
on the Enhanced Fujita scale
Path length12.55 miles (20.20 km)
Highest winds140 mph (230 km/h)
Overall effects
Fatalities0
Injuries22
Economic losses$300 million (2020 USD)
Areas affectedJonesboro and areas east of Brookland, Arkansas, US
Part of the Tornadoes of 2020
In the afternoon of March 28, 2020, a large and intense [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") moved through [Craighead County, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craighead_County,_Arkansas "Craighead County, Arkansas"), United States, striking the eastern portions of [Jonesboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonesboro,_Arkansas "Jonesboro, Arkansas"). The tornado, which was on the ground for 16 minutes and tracked for 12.55 miles (20.20 km), injured 22 people and damaged an estimated 300 buildings. The tornado, rated EF3 on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale"), heavily damaged planes and hangars at the [Jonesboro Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonesboro_Municipal_Airport "Jonesboro Municipal Airport") and damaged [The Mall at Turtle Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mall_at_Turtle_Creek "The Mall at Turtle Creek") beyond repair. The tornado was captured widely on video, being seen on [traffic cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_camera "Traffic camera") and tower cameras that were shown to the public during live coverage of the event. The tornado first touched down at 4:58 pm [Central Daylight Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") (CDT) reaching EF2 intensity as it impacted a retail area. The tornado continued to strengthen as it neared The Mall at Turtle Creek, which sustained heavy damage. To the northeast, the tornado reached EF3 intensity at it directly impacted the Jonesboro Municipal Airport, where hangars were destroyed and a [Beechcraft King Air 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beechcraft_King_Air "Beechcraft King Air") was blown down the airport's [runway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway "Runway"). At a railroad located to the northeast, 112 railcars were blown off. The tornado slightly wavered in intensity at this location. Continuing to track to the northeast, it again reached EF3 intensity as it struck a subdivision of homes. Wind speeds as the tornado struck the homes were estimated to have been as high as 140 miles per hour (230 km/h). The tornado then began to consistently weaken, dissipating 16 minutes after touching down. Advanced forecasting -------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Jonesboro_tornado&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Advanced forecasting")\] On March 25, meteorologists working for the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) outlined a "slight", level 2-out-of-5 risk of severe weather in northern [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), western [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), southeastern [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas") and a small portion of [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-1) The following day, on March 26, the SPC moved the slight risk slightly northward, putting northern Arkansas in a "marginal", level 1-out-of-5 risk but moving it out of the slight risk area.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:7-2) The SPC also outlined a 5% risk of tornadoes for northern Oklahoma and southern Kansas, while a 2% risk of tornadoes existed from central Oklahoma to central Missouri.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:7-2) The Day 3 convective outlook outlined on March 26 showed southeastern Arkansas in a slight risk area, although Jonesboro remained in a marginal risk.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-3) [![Image 3: A map of the central and southern United States, with several Arkansas counties states red, indicating a tornado watch. Below are tornado probabilities and the NOAA logo.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Tornado_Watch_68%2C_March_28%2C_2020.jpg/250px-Tornado_Watch_68%2C_March_28%2C_2020.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tornado_Watch_68,_March_28,_2020.jpg) Tornado Watch #68, which covered much of Arkansas, preceded the tornado The Day 1 convective outlook on March 28 saw the majority of Arkansas put in a slight risk area, with the SPC outlining a 5% chance of tornadoes in northeastern Arkansas. In addition, 15% risks were introduced for both hail and wind, covering much of Arkansas in conjunction with the slight risk area.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-Storm_Prediction-4) To the north, a "moderate", level 4-out-of-5 risk was outlined for [Central Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Illinois "Central Illinois") and extreme eastern [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), which was driven by a 15% risk of tornadoes within 25 miles of a given point, commonly known as a "hatched area".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-Storm_Prediction-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-5) In a 20:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") update convective outlook on March 28, Arkansas was introduced to an expansion of the initial 5% tornado risk, which now covered the eastern half of the state. An "enhanced", level 3-out-of-5 risk was outlined for the [Missouri Bootheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Bootheel "Missouri Bootheel") and small portions of northern Arkansas. A 30% risk for damaging winds was also expanded southward, stretching into northern Arkansas.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-6) Later on March 28, Tornado Watch #68 was issued for much of Arkansas. The tornado watch outlined a moderate risk of tornadoes, but a low risk of EF2+ tornadoes.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-7) The tornado first touched down just east of McClellan Drive at 4:58 pm CDT, moving to the northeast. The tornado initially produced EF0-consistent damage before reaching EF1 intensity on Spencer Circle. EF2 intensity was reached as the tornado impacted the intersection of Race Street and South Caraway Road.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:2-8) At 2801 South Caroway Road, a video showed the tornado impacting and destroying the Gateway Tire and Service Center; a damage study by engineers [Timothy P. Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_P._Marshall "Timothy P. Marshall") and Garry Woodall noted the building was "blown apart" and pieces of the building struck power lines, causing [power flashes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_flash "Power flash").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:5-9) On the southern edge of the tornado's path, a building suffered a wall failure.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-10) To the north, a large [steel building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_building "Steel building") suffered a progressive [structural collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_collapse "Structural collapse") as it was directly by the tornado, which at the time maintained wind speeds as high as 131 miles per hour (211 km/h).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-11) The tornado wavered in strength as it crossed over Stone Street, producing EF1 damage to an office building.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13) A post office in the area lost its roof, and several retail outlets were damaged by the tornado.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:5-9) [![Image 4: A map with several polygons and lines showing the tornado's strength at a given location](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Jonesboro_tornado_peak_intensity.png/250px-Jonesboro_tornado_peak_intensity.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jonesboro_tornado_peak_intensity.png) Track and intensity map of the tornado through the Jonesboro Municipal Airport. The tornado re-intensified as it crossed East Highland Drive, reaching EF3 intensity above a subdivision of homes and destroying at least one home southwest of the [Jonesboro Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonesboro_Municipal_Airport "Jonesboro Municipal Airport").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-14) The tornado then entered [The Mall at Turtle Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mall_at_Turtle_Creek "The Mall at Turtle Creek"), heavily damaging the building and collapsing several walls in varying directions.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:52-15) The mall flooded following the tornado.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-16) The tornado maintained 148-mile-per-hour (238 km/h) wind speeds as it drew closer to the airport, where another steel building collapsed under the tornadic winds.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-17) On the grounds of the Jonesboro Municipal Airport, the tornado inflicted EF3 damage to steel buildings and hangars north of the [tarmac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway "Runway"); at least one plane was overturned.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-19) [The Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_Owners_and_Pilots_Association "Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association") noted that 50 aircraft were damaged at the airport and that a [Beechcraft King Air 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beechcraft_King_Air "Beechcraft King Air") was blown down the runway by the tornado.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:4-20) A maintenance hangar owned by Fly Jonesboro was also destroyed.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:4-20) It weakened to EF2 intensity on Lindbergh Drive before entering a large neighborhood of homes on and to the north of Yukon Drive. At least one home was damaged at EF2 intensity on Wildwood Point.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:0-21)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13) To the north of the airport, the tornado derailed 112 railcars off of a railroad.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:5-9) [![Image 5: A collapsed metal building, with a foundation and metal beams visible](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Gateway_Tire_and_Service_leveled_at_high-end_EF2_by_the_Jonesboro_tornado.jpg/250px-Gateway_Tire_and_Service_leveled_at_high-end_EF2_by_the_Jonesboro_tornado.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gateway_Tire_and_Service_leveled_at_high-end_EF2_by_the_Jonesboro_tornado.jpg) The collapsed Gateway Tire and Service on South Caroway Road in Jonesboro On Wildwood Lane, the tornado again reached EF3 intensity, inflicting EF3-rated damage to homes.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:0-21) The tornado maintained this intensity while tracking over Tiffany Lane and over Prospect Road, where a home was destroyed at EF3 intensity; the tornado had estimated wind speeds of 140 miles per hour (230 km/h) at this location.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:0-21) The tornado then crossed Elizabeth Lane, before impacting a few homes on Nathan Drive. On the corner of Nathan Drive and Tawn Drive, at least one home was completely destroyed at EF3 intensity.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:0-21)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13) The tornado weakened after crossing Troy Cove, where EF2 damage was inflicted to a home.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:0-21) The tornado then crossed the Murray Creek and impacted Smithfield Drive, where it entered another subdivision of homes. On Slimbridge Drive and Laura Lea Drive, at least three homes were deroofed at EF2 intensity.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-22) The tornado continued to weaken, dropping to EF1 intensity as it tracked over a field south of Darrick Circle, before re-reaching EF2 intensity as it impacted and tracked parallel to [U.S. Route 49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_49 "U.S. Route 49") and East Johnson Avenue. A small building located off the highway partially collapsed in wind speeds estimated to have been as high as 135 miles per hour (217 km/h).[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-23) Further to the northeast, a steel building was heavily damaged at EF2 intensity.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-24)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13) Traffic camera video of the tornado in Jonesboro A short distance northeast, the tornado weakened to EF1 intensity, moving to the east and clipping Jonesboro Junction. A home located on County Road 928 received EF1 damage, being directly impacted by the tornado.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-25) The tornado began to track through less-populated areas near the end of its life, only striking a subdivision of homes on Eason Street and Dooley Street. The tornado crossed the three-way intersection of County Road 933 and County Road 938 and later County Roads 936 and 939 while beginning to become thinner. Shortly after tracking over [Arkansas Highway 230](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_Highway_230 "Arkansas Highway 230") the tornado weakened to EF0 intensity before dissipating east of [Aetna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aetna,_Craighead_County,_Arkansas "Aetna, Craighead County, Arkansas") in [Craighead County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craighead_County,_Arkansas "Craighead County, Arkansas") at 5:14 pm CDT.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13) The tornado was on the ground for 12.55 miles (20.20 km), reaching a maximum width of 600 yards (550 m). The tornado injured 22 people and received an EF3 rating by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") (NWS),[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-26)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13) with maximum wind speeds estimated to have been approximately 140 miles per hour (230 km/h).[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-27) News channel _[KAIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KAIT "KAIT")_ broadcast live video of the tornado, helping warn the public in advance.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:5-9) ### Damage and casualties \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Jonesboro_tornado&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Damage and casualties")\] The tornado damaged or destroyed many buildings in and around Jonesboro. The tornado caused monetary damage that totaled an estimated $300 million (2020 [USD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")).[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-28) In addition to structural and monetary figures, 22 people were injured in the tornado.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-29) The lack of fatalities was attributed to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Arkansas "COVID-19 pandemic in Arkansas"), which led to public spaces being less crowded than usual and residents already being in their homes.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:8-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-31) Two of the injured stayed in the hospital overnight, but nobody sustained life-threatening injuries.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-32) The NWS was praised on social media platform [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") (at the time called Twitter) for its advanced warnings of the event, including a tornado warning that was issued ten minutes before the tornado actually touched down. In addition to advanced warnings, the tornado was covered live on television and warnings were transmitted via the [NOAA Weather Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_Weather_Radio "NOAA Weather Radio") outlet, which according to _[Midland Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midland_Radio "Midland Radio")_ "undoubtedly saved lives".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:8-30) [![Image 6: A man in blue clothes and a white hard hat walks up on a pile of debris from an EF5 tornado in 2013](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/EF5Moore1.jpg/250px-EF5Moore1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EF5Moore1.jpg) Timothy P. Marshall (seen in 2013) conducted an in-depth survey of buildings damaged by the tornado In November 2022, structural engineers [Timothy P. Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_P._Marshall "Timothy P. Marshall") and Gary Woodall for the Haag Engineering Company conducted a detailed [damage survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_damage_survey "Tornado damage survey") on the tornado.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-33) The survey, titled "Damage survey of the Jonesboro, Arkansas tornado: March 28, 2020" noted that cleanup efforts began immediately after the tornado, which made surveying of tornado damage difficult.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:6-34) The survey used [Google Street View](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Street_View "Google Street View") and other historical imagery to compare the damaged buildings to their pre-tornado state.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:6-34) One of the buildings surveyed was [Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheddar%27s_Scratch_Kitchen "Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen"), which was directly impacted by the tornado.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:9-35) The building was wood and steel-framed with large windows extending along the building's northern side. The windows blew inward during the tornado, compromising the interior of the structure and lifting up the roof. The survey determined that wind speeds at this location reached 110 miles per hour (180 km/h), which corresponds to an upper-end EF1 rating.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:9-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-36) In October 2021, Cheddar's Scratch Kitchen was reopened to the public after being rebuilt; 25 of the original employees returned to work at the restaurant.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-37) The tornado was described by _[Weather Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Underground_/(weather_service/) "Weather Underground (weather service)")_ as "the first U.S. weather disaster of the [coronavirus-shutdown era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns")".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-38) [Rick Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Crawford_/(politician/) "Rick Crawford (politician)"), state representative for the area, stated that “in the midst of this response, maintaining the appropriate posture with regard to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") is going to be an added challenge”; the pandemic was affecting Arkansas at the time of the tornado.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-39) The City of Jonesboro ordered a 7 pm [curfew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curfew "Curfew").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:2-8) [Heart to Heart International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_to_Heart_International "Heart to Heart International") and other humanitarian groups like the [International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement") helped with recovery efforts in Jonesboro,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-40)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-41) as well as first responders and emergency personnel from the region.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:3-42) [Bay, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay,_Arkansas "Bay, Arkansas") Police Chief Paul Keith stated that “After the tornado passed, \[the area\] was inundated with first responders from all over".[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:3-42) StormPoint, a non-profit group, flew a drone to survey and capture imagery of the tornado's damage path, which was conducted to aid the Jonesboro Police Department.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:4-20) Several weaker tornadoes were associated with the storm system that produced the Jonesboro tornado.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Jonesboro_tornado#cite_note-:1-13)
List of confirmed tornadoes – Saturday, March 28, 2020[note 1]

EFUNW of EvandaleBlack HawkIowa42°28′21″N 92°18′50″W﻿ / ﻿42.4725°N 92.3138°W22:55–22:560.32 mi (0.51 km)20 yd (18 m)A tornado occurred in an unpopulated near the Waterloo Waste Water Treatment Plant along the Cedar River. While tree damage may have occurred, no damage was reported.[50]

One person was indirectly injured after stepping on broken glass after the tornado dissipated.[52]
EF0E of MaynardFayetteIowa42°45′09″N 91°51′19″W﻿ / ﻿42.7525°N 91.8552°W23:40–23:433.6 mi (5.8 km)50 yd (46 m)A weak tornado caused minor damage at several farms.[53]
EFUESE of Andover to ENE of CambridgeHenryIllinois41°17′N 90°14′W﻿ / ﻿41.28°N 90.24°W00:43–00:441.07 mi (1.72 km)10 yd (9.1 m)A brief tornado was photographed but did no observable damage.[54]
EF2Corydon to W of SpottsvilleHendersonKentucky37°44′30″N 87°42′14″W﻿ / ﻿37.7418°N 87.7038°W00:58–01:1216.79 mi (27.02 km)500 yd (460 m)This low-end EF2 tornado downed trees in Corydon before moving through the southern fringes of Henderson. Dozens of homes sustained roof, siding, fascia, and soffit damage, and over a dozen barns and outbuildings sustained roof or structural damage. One large, well-built barn was completely destroyed with the debris scattered across a field. Federal disaster declaration approved for March 28 Jonesboro tornado
====================================================================

![Image 1: “I really believe the airport is going to come back better than ever,” said Saul.](https://gray-kait-prod.gtv-cdn.com/resizer/v2/J6INYPPRLVDQZHAAHMHWXFY4OM.png?auth=ca7180f0ff7828e07c4b2fec930c88fceb6d740bc720f2c6632df86c52f274c3&width=800&height=450&smart=true)

“I really believe the airport is going to come back better than ever,” said Saul.(KAIT)

By Region 8 Newsdesk

Updated: May 9, 2020 at 2:56 PM CDT

JONESBORO, Ark. (KAIT) - The people and businesses impacted by the March 28 tornado in Jonesboro and Craighead County will be able to receive federal disaster aid under a declaration approved this week in the nation’s capital.

According to a media release from Sens. John Boozman and Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) and Rep. Rick Crawford (R-Jonesboro), President Donald Trump [approved a major disaster declaration for Jonesboro and Craighead County](https://www.fema.gov/news-release/2020/05/08/president-donald-j-trump-approves-major-disaster-declaration-arkansas) due to the storms.

State officials had sought the federal help in April, saying Jonesboro had an estimated $500 million in damages due to the storms.

“We are pleased with this quick response from the administration which will provide financial assistance to speed up recovery efforts in the wake of the devastating tornado and severe storms that hit Craighead County. President Trump’s swift action to approve the state’s request for a disaster declaration is appreciated given the economic toll that the COVID-19 pandemic has already taken on the state of Arkansas,” Boozman, Cotton, Crawford said in the letter, which was signed by the other members of the delegation - Reps. French Hill (R-Little Rock), Steve Womack (R-Rogers) and Bruce Westerman (R-Hot Springs).

Back in April, [county emergency officials said the declaration](https://www.kait8.com/2020/04/24/federal-disaster-declaration-sought-march-jonesboro-tornado/) would help not only residents but government agencies and utilities like Jonesboro Municipal Airport, City Water & Light and Craighead Electric, with losses that are not covered by insurance or other federal funding.

The funding will also include help for homeowners or renters to cover losses not covered by insurance, officials said.

=========================================================

Abstract
--------

On March 28, 2020, a tornado developed in southeast Jonesboro and traveled northeast through the city damaging about 300 buildings. There were 22 injuries but fortunately, no fatalities, which is remarkable given that the tornado traveled through a densely populated area on Saturday afternoon. The next day, the authors surveyed the damage assigning degrees of damage (DoD) to multiple damage indicators (DIs) in accordance with the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale (WSEC, 2006). The EF-Scale was written in 2006 and adopted by the National Weather Service (NWS) in 2007. In this event, NWS personnel plotted the damage locations on the damage assessment toolkit (DAT) and assigned a maximum damage rating of EF 3 to this tornado.

... Read more

Key takeaways

![Image 7: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)AI




-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  The tornado on March 28, 2020, resulted in damage to approximately 300 buildings in Jonesboro, AR.
2.  The tornado reached a maximum damage rating of EF 3, with an estimated wind speed of 61 m/s (136 mph).
3.  Damage surveys revealed the tornado path extended 20 km (12.6 mi) and had a maximum width of 550 m (1800 ft).
4.  Documentation of large shopping malls is lacking; this survey aims to address that for the EF-scale update.
5.  The survey involved more than 80 scientists to standardize the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale for future tornado assessments.

On May 4, 2007, a wide and extremely violent tornado struck Greensburg, KS destroying over 90 percent of the town. Eleven people died. Within days after the event, the author conducted detailed aerial and ground damage surveys assigning EF-scale values to each house. This paper summarizes the findings from the damage survey.

This outbreak, with 62 confirmed fatalities, is considered the deadliest since the May 31, 1985 tornado outbreak that affected Southern Ontario, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and upstate New York. This research is based on damage data collected from Madison and Macon counties in Tennessee using the Visualizing Impacts of Earthquakes with Satellites (VIEWS) system developed by ImageCat, Inc. Enhanced-Fujita (EF) Scale damage ratings were assigned to provide detailed per-building damage assessments which indicate various levels of wind force. [Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

31st Conference on Severe Local Storms, 2025

On 21 March 2022, multiple supercells produced 17 tornadoes in North Texas. The strongest tornado was an EF-3 which occurred in Jack County and struck the City of Jacksboro. The tornado traveled 55.6 km (34.5 miles) and damaged or destroyed dozens of wood-framed residences, an elementary school, and high school. Large span gymnasiums at both schools sustained severe damage. This paper will summarize observations from our damage survey including a discussion of the Enhanced Fujita Scale.

[Damage survey of the North Texas Tornadoes: 26 December 2015](https://www.academia.edu/34321619/Damage_survey_of_the_North_Texas_Tornadoes_26_December_2015)

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

A tornado outbreak occurred during the evening of 26 December 2015 across portions of North Texas. In all, there were 12 confirmed tornadoes in 8 counties. Unfortunately, 13 people lost their lives and there were numerous injuries as two of the strongest tornadoes struck Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) suburbs. Most fatalities occurred in vehicles near the Interstate 30/George Bush Turnpike interchange in Garland, Texas (Fig. 1). Damage survey teams were dispatched the next day by the Fort Worth National Weather Service (FWD) to determine characteristics of the tornado paths. The survey team utilized the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale to rate damage severity developed by the Wind Science and Engineering Research Center (WSERC, 2006). This scale lists increasing degrees of damage (DoDs) to 28 damage indicators (DIs). DIs involved various building types as well as other items. The EF scale was adopted by the National Weather Service (NWS) in 2007. Not surprisingly, we found that tornadoes exploited construction deficiencies in building connections, sometimes causing more severe building damage. Therefore, we adjusted EF ratings downward where there was poor construction. The damage survey team found two major tornado tracks near Dallas, Texas. One tornado traveled from Midlothian to Ovilla to Glenn Heights and will be referred to herein as the MOG tornado. This tornado traveled 14 km, was up to 110 m wide, with maximum damage intensity of EF3. The other major tornado, produced by a second supercell, traveled from Sunnyvale to Garland to Rowlett and will be referred to herein as the SGR tornado. This tornado traveled about 21 km, was up to 500 m wide, with maximum damage intensity of EF4.

The 20 May 2013 tornado affected the cities of Newcastle, Moore, and Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. The official path length for the tornado, as recorded in Storm Data, was 22.28 km (13.85 mi) and was up to 1,737 m (1,900 yards) wide. The tornado killed 24 people, injured 212 others, and damaged over 4,000 structures, with over 1,000 structures having damage exceeding EF2 intensity. A team of surveyors from the National Weather Center (NWC; University of Oklahoma, CIMMS, National Severe Storms Laboratory, the Norman National Weather Service Forecast Office and the Warning Decision Training Branch) and twoprivate organizations (Haag Engineering and Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety) began surveying tornado damage on 21 May 2013 and continued the survey process for the next several weeks. In this paper we describe the effort to organize the ground survey teams immediately following the event, provide an overview of the tornado evolution, and review specific aspects of the damage survey (in particular, assigning EF5 ratings to residential structures). We will present comparisons of the tornado path and damage to data from several nearby radar facilities.

This paper presents a summary of two decades of damage survey work by the author in studying building damage in the wake of tornadoes. Assigning F scale numbers to structures based on the degree of damage is a subjective visual procedure. However, when trying to derive the intensity of the winds, it is important to consider how well the buildings are constructed and to recognize weak links or flaws within such structures. Large variability’s in the strength of wood-framed buildings will yield an F scale number with no greater confidence than plus or minus one F scale. This paper reveals some of the "fatal flaws" in building construction causing buildings to fail at much lower wind speeds than shown in the current F-scale ranges.

The results depict the physical distribution of the damaging forces away from the centerline of the tornado. FAQs
----

![Image 9: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)AI

What were the maximum wind speeds associated with the damage in Jonesboro tornado?add

The tornado exhibited maximum damage intensity rated EF 3, with expected failure wind speeds around 61 m/s (136 mph) in the large shopping mall.

How was damage intensity assessed in the Jonesboro tornado survey?add

The damage assessment utilized multiple damage indicators (DIs) rated according to the Enhanced Fujita scale, allowing for estimated failure wind speeds for various structures.

What unique challenges occurred during the damage survey after the tornado?add

Immediate cleanup activities complicated the survey, as visible damage details became perishable due to debris removal and repair efforts shortly after the tornado struck.

Which buildings experienced the most severe damage based on the survey findings?add

The most severe damage was noted at the Jonesboro Municipal Airport and to the Ulta and Kirkland retail stores, with some facilities collapsing completely under high wind speeds.

What is the significance of the updated EF-scale regarding this tornado's damage assessment?add

This event highlighted the need for better documentation of large shopping malls and the addition of new damage indicators, as current EF-scale revisions were in progress at the time.

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall15)

30th Conference on Severe Local Storms, 2022

On the evening of March 2-3, 2020, a supercell storm produced 10 tornadoes in-a-row from near Bradford to Lancing, Tennessee. The longest tornado track was the fourth in the series and traveled 102 km (63.13 mi) through the cities of Nashville, Donelson, Hermitage, Mount Juliet, and Lebanon, paralleling Interstate 40. The tornado caused 5 deaths and about 220 injuries. This paper summarizes the findings from our damage survey, herein called the Nashville tornado. The authors spent several days traveling the damage path and documented the degree of damage (DoD) to specific damage indicators (DIs) using the EF damage scale (WERC, 2006). The EF-scale was adopted by the National Weather Service (NWS) in 2007.

downloadDownload free PDF[View PDFchevron\_right](https://www.academia.edu/91310040/Damage_Survey_of_the_Nashville_TN_Tornado_3_March_2020)

[20 May 2013 Moore, Oklahoma, Tornado: Damage Survey and Analysis](https://www.academia.edu/34321100/20_May_2013_Moore_Oklahoma_Tornado_Damage_Survey_and_Analysis)

[Donald W Burgess](https://ou.academia.edu/DonaldBurgess), [Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

The tornado that affected Moore, Oklahoma, and the surrounding area on 20 May 2013 was an extreme event. It traveled 23 km and damage was up to 1.7 km wide. The tornado killed 24 people, injured over 200 others, and damaged many structures. A team of surveyors from the Norman, Oklahoma, National Weather Center and two private companies performed a detailed survey (all objects/structures) of the tornado to provide better documentation than is normally done, in part to aid future studies of the event. The team began surveying tornado damage on the morning of 21 May and continued the survey process for the next several weeks. Extensive ground surveys were performed. The surveys were aided by use of high-resolution aerial and satellite imagery. The survey process utilized the enhanced Fujita (EF) scale and was facilitated by use of a National Weather Service (NWS) software package: the Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT). The survey team defined a ''well built'' house that qualified for an EF5 rating. Survey results document 4253 objects damaged by the tornado, 4222 of them EF-scale damage indicators (DIs). Of the total DIs, about 50% were associated with EF0 ratings. Excluding EF0 damage, 38% were associated with EF1, 24% with EF2, 21% with EF3, 17% with EF4, and only 0.4% associated with EF5. For the strongest level of damage (EF5), only nine homes were found. Survey results are similar to other documented tornadoes, but the amount of EF1 damage is greater than in other cases. Also discussed is the use of non-DI objects that are damaged and ways in which to improve future surveys.

[Damage Survey of the Mayfield, KY Tornado: 10 December 2021](https://www.academia.edu/90132303/Damage_Survey_of_the_Mayfield_KY_Tornado_10_December_2021)

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall15)

30th Conference on Severe Local Storms, 2022

On December 10, 2021, a tornado outbreak occurred in the southern U.S. with more than 70 tornadoes reported. The worst hit areas were northeast Arkansas, western Tennessee, western Kentucky, and southern Illinois. This paper will concentrate on the damage in western Kentucky, particularly the towns of Mayfield and Dawson Springs where the most severe damage occurred. A detailed damage survey was conducted in the days following this event and the National Weather Service rated this tornado EF 4 on the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale. Various degrees of damage (DoD) were assigned to different damage indicators (DIs) in accordance with the 2006 EF-scale (WERC, 2006).

[Damage Survey of the Joplin Tornado: 22 May 2011](https://www.academia.edu/25105205/Damage_Survey_of_the_Joplin_Tornado_22_May_2011)

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

On 22 May 2011, a large and destructive tornado traveled through southern portions of Joplin, MO, a city of approximately 50,000 people. According to the Storm Data, the tornado killed 158 people and injured more than 1000. Total property damage exceeded two billion dollars. This paper summarizes the results of our damage survey. The EF-scale was utilized on several building types.

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

On 4 May 1999, the Wind Science and Engineering Research Center at Texas Tech University dispatched three survey teams to the Oklahoma City area to conduct a tornado damage survey. The author was the leader of one of the teams whose purpose was to survey tornado damage in and around the suburb of Moore, Oklahoma. The survey team was given five tasks: 1) to map out the damage path and assign F-scale numbers to damaged buildings, 2) to document the performance of housing, 3) to interview witnesses, 4) to document projectiles, and 5) to assess the performance of any above-or belowground shelters within the damage path. This paper will present the methodology utilized for conducting the tornado damage survey and will summarize the observations and findings of the survey team. Wind speeds necessary to cause the observed damage to residences were found to be significantly lower than the established F-scale wind speeds. The author returned to the disaster area three months later and discovered that, in general, the quality of new home construction had not improved.

downloadDownload free PDF[View PDFchevron\_right](https://www.academia.edu/25105784/Tornado_damage_survey_at_Moore_Oklahoma)

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

On 31 May 2013, an intense, multiple-vortex tornado meandered through sparsely populated areas near El Reno, Oklahoma. This exceptionally wide tornado had a complex path, changing rapidly in both speed and direction. The tornado killed eight people, all in vehicles, including three severe storm researchers. This paper summarizes our findings from conducting a damage survey using the EF (Enhanced Fujita) scale developed by the Wind Science and Engineering Center. Survey teams also documented damage to 344 non-standard DIs which included 112 oil tank batteries. The maximum damage rating was determined to be EF3. Total path length was 26.2 km.

[Tim Marshall](https://independent.academia.edu/TimMarshall6)

Investigation of buildings damaged from the Mesquite, Texas tornado revealed several interesting features in the debris pattern. Most of the debris was scattered northward with little rotation. Tornado characteristics which effect the debris pattern will be discussed. Some residences in the tornados' path were heavily damaged while adjacent homes remained unscathed. It will be shown how the variability in construction practices effected building performance. Attention to details like the installation of anchor bolts or metal straps helped explain large variations in the damage zone. Performance of residences was directly related to the type and amount of anchorage used and how well they were installed. Four primary connection failures were observed: wall/foundation, wall stud/bottom plate, roof joist/top plate, and rafter/top plate. Suggestions are presented to help minimize structural damage in high winds.

This field campaign, undertaken in the aftermath of the 2008 ‘Super Tuesday’ tornadoes, was funded by MCEER and Texas Tech University’s Wind Science and Engineering Research Center. It presented the team with a unique opportunity to collect geographically located perishable damage data on a per-building level throughout a variety of tornado strengths and environments. This exploration marks the first tornado event where the VIEWS (Visualizing Impacts of Earthquakes with Satellites) system has been deployed to collect detailed ground survey data for identification and mapping of damage in a wideranging area. This use again extends the original aim of the VIEWS system and shows its flexibility for multi-hazard damage detection. On May 10, 2008, a large, fast-moving tornado struck Picher, OK, a small town in the northeast part of the state. The town was part of a HAZMAT site due to mine tailings that contaminated the environment. The tornado destroyed many of the remaining buildings, including a large number of manufactured homes. In this paper, the author presents the results of the damage survey.

JONESBORO ARKANSAS TORNADO 2020: A WARNING SUCCESS STORY
========================================================

![Image 3: tornado in sky](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0531/2856/0817/articles/1daf482d2ba735a10d06889e2cde584c_aabd7eb2-ab14-4c8f-9c36-7585ed539fc2.jpg?v=1746477120&width=1800)

Table of Contents
-----------------

*   [No Fatalities Reported](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story?srsltid=AfmBOoqt1vH9gTEtePKN2e21zQ029IyVImbSRqBSb-doarXsSA9iP5D5#no-fatalities-reported)
*   [Tracking the Tornado](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story?srsltid=AfmBOoqt1vH9gTEtePKN2e21zQ029IyVImbSRqBSb-doarXsSA9iP5D5#tracking-the-tornado)
*   [Early Warning Was Key](https://midlandusa.com/blogs/blog/jonesboro-arkansas-tornado-a-warning-success-story?srsltid=AfmBOoqt1vH9gTEtePKN2e21zQ029IyVImbSRqBSb-doarXsSA9iP5D5#early-warning-was-key)

A Tornado Warning Success Story
===============================

On Saturday, March 28, 2020, ten minutes after the National Weather Service issued its warning, a strong tornado with top winds estimated at 140mph, plowed a twelve mile long path through portions of Jonesboro, AR. The Jonesboro Arkansas Tornado in 2020 damaged or destroyed more than 200 homes and businesses, including Turtle Creek Mall and the city airport.

No Fatalities Reported
----------------------

Eighteen people were injured, but amazingly, no one was killed. Isolation due to the COVID-19 coronavirus meant the mall and other businesses were much less crowded than they would have been on a typical Saturday afternoon. Most importantly, the tornado warning was issued at 4:47 pm and the twister touched down at 4:57pm, meaning those ten minutes allowed everyone plenty of time to seek shelter and survive.

Tracking the Tornado
--------------------

The National Weather Service damage survey found that the twister touched down just north of Interstate highway 555, produced EF-2 damage at the Mall, then strengthened to EF-3 force as it destroyed buildings and airplanes at the Jonesboro Airport and beyond. At its widest, the funnel left a swath of damage one-third of a mile across, along a path of more than twelve miles.

Early Warning Was Key
---------------------

Occurring on a March day (the middle of Arkansas’ tornado season), just before 5pm (the most common time of day for Arkansas tornadoes), and two hours after Tornado Watch #68 had been issued for the area, the tornado was not unexpected, meaning the people of Jonesboro were well aware of the day’s severe weather risk. Warnings from the National Weather Service via weather radio and cell phone, combined with outstanding on-air coverage by local television and radio stations undoubtedly saved lives. As the 2020 tornado season kicks in, everyone can learn a good lesson from the Jonesboro tornado: know your risk for severe weather, have multiple redundant methods of receiving warnings, watch your local TV station’s storm coverage, and have a practiced, well-understood plan of action to get to your safe place.  
  
Every home, school, and business should have a [Midland NOAA Weather Alert Radio](https://midlandusa.com/collections/weather).  As the official “Voice of the National Weather Service”, it keeps you informed and alerted no matter what you’re doing. Buy it, plug it in, and be prepared.

Firefighters remember Jonesboro tornado four years later
========================================================

By [Macy Davis](https://www.kait8.com/authors/macy-davis/)

Published: Mar. 28, 2024 at 10:55 PM CDT

JONESBORO, Ark. (KAIT) - It’s been four years since an EF-3 tornado made its way through Jonesboro, leaving neighborhoods destroyed and tearing through some city businesses.

On March 28, 2020, the tornado injured 22 people, according to emergency personnel. It also left many without a home.

One of those people was Lucas Luster, a driver at the Jonesboro Fire Department. He remembers that day, four years ago, vividly.

He called his family to let them know a storm was developing in Jonesboro.

Luster said his family had no idea how bad it would be. They kept an eye on the tornado once it touched down.

“Ryan Vaughan was staying with it, which is great because I had no idea. So, I called my family as soon as he said it was headed northeast,” Luster said.

Luster called his wife after that and told her and their kids to take shelter.

He was on the phone with his wife when the tornado hit, he heard the storm take out windows. Then, the phone went dead.

After the call with his wife, Luster was in a state of shock. He was getting his bearings, trying to figure out what he needed to do when he got a call from another firefighter.

“They said, look, your house is gone,” Luster said. “But everybody’s alive. Everybody’s okay.”

After making sure his family was okay, Luster had to go out and do his job as a firefighter. That’s something Jonesboro Fire Chief Marty Hamrick had to do as well.

He was watching movies with his family when he learned of the tornado and had to respond.

“I’m like, hon’, I’ve got to go. I’ve got a job to do, and I don’t know when I’ll be back,” Hamrick said. “Because the way it looked on TV and knowing that part of town it looked like it was going through, we were expecting a lot of injuries and deaths.”

Thankfully, no one died in the tornado. All hands were on deck when the tornado hit.

Jonesboro Fire sent out a call bringing in all four personnel.

First responders were constantly working to make sure people were recovered.

According to Hamrick, by the next day, everybody was accounted for.

Despite the chaos and tragedy of the event, Chief Hamrick said it’s helped the department prepare for future severe weather.

“We definitely have a good game plan now of how we’re going to handle it,” Hamrick added. “The biggest piece is identifying staging areas for all the help that’s going to come in.”

As Luster reflects four years later, he’s grateful for the safety of his family and the help of the community.
